pathway.title: JavaScript Programming
pathway.description: Learn to plan, write, test, and explain small JavaScript programs using clear steps, data, functions, and modules.

course.title: JavaScript Programming — Intermediate
course.short_description: An intermediate JavaScript course on scope, functional design, collection pipelines, modular testing, validation, promises, concurrency, and safe local JSON workflows.
course.prerequisites: Completion of JavaScript Programming — Beginner or equivalent experience with variables, functions, arrays, objects, modules, error handling, and Node.js scripts.
learning_outcomes: Use scope, closures, pure functions, and callbacks to design reusable behavior with explicit state boundaries.
Transform and query arrays and objects with collection methods while controlling mutation and validating assumptions.
Organize ES modules, test observable contracts, and model input validation and error behavior.
Use promises, async/await, and concurrency primitives with explicit failure and resource-limit decisions.
Build a local JSON-file adapter that validates parsed records and clearly documents persistence limitations.
course.dependencies: Node.js 20+ built-ins only; no third-party packages required.

modules.title: Design reusable functions and state boundaries
modules.description: Reason about scope, closures, pure calculations, side effects, and callbacks.

topics.title: Understand lexical scope and closures
topics.description: Trace where identifiers are available and use a closure to preserve private state.

lesson.title: Understand lexical scope and closures
objectives: Distinguish global, function, and block scope.
Explain how a closure retains access to its lexical environment.
Use a closure for a small private-state example and identify its limits.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Scope answers a practical question: where can code refer to a name? A `let` or `const` declared inside a block is available only within that block; a function parameter and local binding belong to that function call. Lexical scope means JavaScript decides access from where functions are written, not from which caller happens to invoke them. A closure occurs when a function keeps access to bindings in its surrounding lexical environment after that outer function has returned. This is useful for small private state, callbacks, and function factories. The counter below returns an inner function, which still sees `count` on later calls. Closures are not encryption: code holding a returned function can still cause its behavior, and a closure can retain memory longer than intended. Prefer a closure when it clarifies ownership, not simply to make code look advanced. Keep state transitions small and test how repeated calls behave.

blocks.alt_text: An outer function creates a local count and returns an inner function that retains access to it.

topics.title: Design pure functions and control side effects
topics.description: Separate predictable calculations from state changes, logging, and file or network effects.

lesson.title: Design pure functions and control side effects
objectives: Describe a pure function in terms of inputs and outputs.
Identify common side effects and hidden dependencies.
Refactor a calculation so callers control when effects occur.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: A pure function produces the same result for the same inputs and does not change state outside itself. For example, adding two values is easy to test because it neither reads the clock nor edits a shared array. A side effect is an observable interaction beyond returning a value: changing an object, writing a file, printing output, or making a request are examples. Side effects are necessary in useful programs, but spreading them through every calculation makes behavior harder to predict. A practical design keeps core transformations pure and places effects at clearly named boundaries. The example returns a summary rather than logging inside the function, so another caller can display it, test it, or combine it with more work. Purity is a design tool, not an absolute rule: a function that deliberately updates a repository may be appropriate when its contract is explicit. Make dependencies visible as parameters where that helps testing.

topics.title: Use callbacks and higher-order functions
topics.description: Pass behavior as a function to make small reusable operations configurable.

lesson.title: Use callbacks and higher-order functions
objectives: Explain that functions are values that can be passed to other functions.
Use a callback with `map`, `filter`, or a custom helper.
Choose a descriptive callback and avoid unnecessary abstraction.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: In JavaScript, functions are values: a variable can refer to one, and another function can receive it as an argument. A higher-order function accepts a function, returns one, or both. A callback is a function supplied so another operation can call it at the appropriate time. Array methods such as `map` and `filter` are familiar examples: they call a provided function for each element. This lets the caller describe the rule while the reusable operation handles iteration. The example accepts a formatting callback, so a caller can choose how a fictional title is presented. A callback is not automatically asynchronous; it may run immediately, later, or repeatedly depending on the receiving function's contract. Read that contract before assuming when it runs or how often. Keep callbacks short and named when their behavior is meaningful. Do not create a generic framework for a single trivial operation; reuse is valuable only when it makes intent clearer.

modules.title: Transform and query structured data
modules.description: Build collection pipelines, order and search records, and safely reshape objects.

topics.title: Transform collections with map, filter, and reduce
topics.description: Build a readable data pipeline by transforming, selecting, and aggregating array values.

lesson.title: Transform collections with map, filter, and reduce
objectives: Use `map` to transform every element and `filter` to select matching elements.
Use `reduce` with an explicit initial value to aggregate data.
Break a data pipeline into named stages and verify intermediate results.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Collection methods express common operations without manual index bookkeeping. `map` transforms each item and preserves the number of items; `filter` keeps items whose predicate returns true; `reduce` combines items into one accumulated value. A pipeline reads from left to right, but each stage should have a clear input and output shape. The example first selects available fictional books, then sums their page counts. Providing an initial value to `reduce` makes the empty-array result well-defined and avoids relying on a first item. These methods do not guarantee deep immutability: a callback can still mutate an object it receives. Prefer returning new values rather than editing shared records unexpectedly. For long pipelines, introduce named intermediate constants so readers can inspect each stage and tests can isolate rules. Check both an ordinary list and an empty list, since empty collections often reveal assumptions hidden by a happy-path example.

topics.title: Sort, search, and test collections safely
topics.description: Use comparators and query methods while protecting the source array from accidental reordering.

lesson.title: Sort, search, and test collections safely
objectives: Write a comparator with a clear ordering rule.
Use `find`, `some`, and `every` for distinct query questions.
Sort a copy or use a copying sort method when the source order must stay unchanged.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Sorting is a comparison problem: the comparator should return a negative value when the first item belongs earlier, zero when they are equivalent for ordering, and a positive value when it belongs later. For numeric fields, subtracting the second value from the first is a common concise comparator; for strings, use a locale-aware comparison when appropriate. The older `sort()` method changes the array it is called on, so clone the array first if its order is part of shared state. Modern runtimes also provide `toSorted()`, which returns a sorted copy; Node.js 20 supports it. Query methods answer different questions: `find` returns the first matching element or `undefined`, `some` asks whether at least one match exists, and `every` asks whether all elements match. None of these methods substitutes for validating external data. Test ties, empty lists, and absent matches to make the intended behavior explicit.

topics.title: Reshape objects with destructuring and safe defaults
topics.description: Extract fields, create updated copies, and distinguish missing values from intentional nulls.

lesson.title: Reshape objects with destructuring and safe defaults
objectives: Use object destructuring to extract named values and defaults.
Use spread syntax to create a shallow updated object.
Apply optional chaining and nullish coalescing without confusing `null` with other falsy values.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Objects are often reshaped as data crosses a boundary. Destructuring gives selected properties local names, while a default applies when a property is `undefined`; it does not replace an explicit `null`. Object spread copies enumerable own properties into a new, shallow object, after which later properties override earlier ones. This is useful for a focused update such as changing availability without modifying the original top-level record. The copy is shallow: nested objects remain shared unless they too are copied. Optional chaining (`?.`) safely stops a property access when the value before it is nullish, and nullish coalescing (`??`) supplies a fallback only for `null` or `undefined`. That differs from `||`, which also treats `0`, `false`, and an empty string as missing. Choose defaults from the data contract, not convenience alone, and validate records before assuming fields exist.

modules.title: Structure and verify modular programs
modules.description: Set module boundaries, test behavior, and validate inputs with explicit error contracts.

topics.title: Organize modules around stable responsibilities
topics.description: Create explicit module boundaries and avoid hidden work during import.

lesson.title: Organize modules around stable responsibilities
objectives: Distinguish named exports from default exports.
Separate reusable functions from command-line or file-system side effects.
Describe how relative module paths and module formats affect Node.js imports.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: An ES module is a file with explicit `import` and `export` declarations. A named export communicates that a file provides one or more deliberate capabilities; a default export offers one primary value but can make the exported name less visible at the import site. Relative imports describe nearby project files, while Node.js built-ins use names such as `node:path`. Keep reusable logic in modules that do not unexpectedly read files or start work just because they were imported. Put command-line parsing, printing, and filesystem calls near an application boundary, then call reusable functions with explicit inputs. This makes code easier to test with invented data and allows a future adapter to change without rewriting every rule. Node.js treats `.mjs` as an ES module; package configuration can also define module behavior for `.js` files. Avoid circular dependencies because they make initialization and ownership harder to follow. A diagram helps reveal which layer is allowed to depend on which other layer.

topics.title: Test behavior with Node.js assert and test runner
topics.description: Build deterministic checks around contracts, edge cases, and isolated effects.

lesson.title: Test behavior with Node.js assert and test runner
objectives: Write assertions for expected values and expected failures.
Use `node:test` to organize independent test cases.
Test public behavior rather than depending on private implementation details.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: A test is an executable claim about behavior. An assertion compares an actual result with an expected one and stops or reports a failure when they differ. Node.js provides `node:assert/strict` for precise checks and `node:test` for organizing test cases without an external package. Tests should be deterministic: avoid relying on the current time, network access, or a particular machine path unless those are controlled. Include normal, boundary, and invalid inputs, then state what each test proves. A unit test can exercise a pure function quickly; an adapter test may use a temporary directory or injected fake so it does not touch learner or school data. Testing only that a helper was called can overfit the implementation, so prefer checking outputs and visible effects required by the contract. A passing suite is evidence for the cases it runs, not proof that every possible input is safe. Keep tests small and named after the behavior they protect.

topics.title: Validate inputs and model expected errors
topics.description: Reject invalid boundary data deliberately and distinguish expected failures from programming defects.

lesson.title: Validate inputs and model expected errors
objectives: Validate type, shape, and domain constraints at an input boundary.
Use a clear error type or result contract for expected invalid input.
Avoid catching and hiding errors that the current layer cannot handle.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: JavaScript's flexible values make boundary validation important: a function may receive `null`, an array, or an object with missing fields even when its author expected a record. Validate external input once near the boundary, then pass a normalized internal shape to the rest of the program. Validation should check both structure and domain rules, such as a non-empty title and a positive integer identifier. Expected invalid input can be reported through a documented return value or a specific error class; callers should know which contract to use. Avoid broad `try...catch` blocks that return a generic success-looking default, because that hides defects and corrupts later reasoning. Catch an error only where the program can respond meaningfully, and preserve enough context without exposing private values. Validation is not a substitute for authorization or security controls in a real service. Use small reusable predicates and test missing, malformed, and boundary cases explicitly.

topics.title: Work with promises and async functions
topics.description: Understand promise states and use async/await to make asynchronous flow readable.

lesson.title: Work with promises and async functions
objectives: Describe pending, fulfilled, and rejected promise outcomes.
Use `async` and `await` to consume an asynchronous result.
Catch expected rejections at a layer that can respond meaningfully.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: A promise represents the eventual outcome of an operation that may finish later. It is pending before completion, fulfilled with a value on success, or rejected with a reason on failure. An `async` function always returns a promise, even when it appears to return a plain value. `await` pauses that async function until the promise settles; it does not freeze the entire Node.js process. A `try...catch` around an awaited operation can handle a rejection, but the handler should add value, such as choosing a safe message or fallback. Do not mistake asynchronous syntax for parallel execution: awaiting one task before starting the next is sequential. Use APIs that return promises and inspect their error behavior rather than inventing timing assumptions. The example uses Node's built-in timer promise to make the delayed result visible without a network or third-party package. Reliable asynchronous code makes success, failure, and timing boundaries explicit.

topics.title: Coordinate concurrency and cancellation safely
topics.description: Choose sequential or concurrent work based on dependencies and define how partial failures behave.

lesson.title: Coordinate concurrency and cancellation safely
objectives: Distinguish independent tasks from dependent sequential tasks.
Use `Promise.all` for independent work that should succeed together.
Explain partial failure, cancellation limits, and why concurrency should be bounded for large workloads.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Asynchronous tasks can overlap when neither depends on the other's result. Starting both promises and awaiting `Promise.all` allows independent work to progress concurrently and returns results in input order when all succeed. If any promise rejects, `Promise.all` rejects, but it does not automatically cancel the other work already started. For independent tasks where partial success is useful, `Promise.allSettled` reports each outcome instead. Some workflows are sequential because the second task needs the first result; parallelizing them would be incorrect. Concurrency is not the same as unlimited fan-out: starting thousands of operations at once can exhaust memory or overwhelm a service. Use a small, deliberate limit when processing large collections, and respect cancellation only when the underlying operation supports it. The example uses local timer promises with different delays, not an external service. Document whether the contract is all-or-nothing, partial results, or fail-fast with outstanding work still running.

items.prompt: When is `Promise.all` a reasonable choice?

choices.text: When each task depends on the previous result
To cancel all running operations automatically
For independent tasks that should succeed together

items.prompt: What happens to other already-started tasks when one Promise.all input rejects?
Why limit concurrency for a very large workload?

Bound large workloads and make partial-failure behavior explicit.

topics.title: Read and write JSON files with async Node.js APIs
topics.description: Validate parsed data, handle missing files deliberately, and keep file persistence behind an adapter.

lesson.title: Read and write JSON files with async Node.js APIs
objectives: Use `node:fs/promises` to read and write UTF-8 files asynchronously.
Distinguish file-system errors from malformed JSON and invalid record shape.
Keep file operations in an adapter and state the limits of a local JSON file.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: JSON is a text format, not a database. `JSON.parse` converts text to JavaScript values but does not prove that the result has the shape your program expects. Validate the root type and each record before using the data. Node's `node:fs/promises` API offers asynchronous file operations; specify UTF-8 when reading text and catch only expected failures such as a missing optional file. A malformed JSON file should be reported rather than silently replaced with an empty collection, because replacement could hide data loss. Writing a full JSON document is suitable for a small local exercise, but simultaneous writers can overwrite each other's changes, and a crash during replacement may leave incomplete data. Production persistence needs deliberate durability, access control, backups, concurrency, and recovery design. Keep serialization and file operations behind a small adapter so domain rules can be tested separately. Use temporary, invented files in exercises; never point lesson code at school or learner records.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.explanation: This runnable example illustrates read and write json files with async node.js apis using fictional or local practice data. Predict the output before running it with Node.js 20+, then change one input and explain how the observed result relates to the stated contract.

blocks.title: Concept flow
blocks.alt_text: A file is read as UTF-8 text, parsed into values, checked for the expected list shape, and only then used; writing serializes first.
blocks.content: file path → async read (UTF-8) → parse JSON → validate shape → use records; write follows serialize → async write

blocks.title: Guided practice
instructions: Implement `loadRecords(filePath)` that returns an empty list only when the file is absent, but reports malformed JSON and invalid record shapes. Write a test with a temporary file containing invented data. Explain why a JSON file does not provide transactions or safe concurrent updates.
success_checks: The result follows an explicit behavior contract and uses descriptive names.
A normal case and a relevant boundary or invalid case are checked.
The learner can explain the diagram, expected output, and one limitation.

items.prompt: What does `JSON.parse` establish?

choices.text: That the text is valid JSON syntax, not that it has the expected application shape

items.prompt: Why not silently replace malformed JSON with an empty list?

choices.text: It can hide corruption or data loss

items.prompt: What is a limitation of a simple JSON-file store?

choices.text: Concurrent writers and crash recovery need additional design

blocks.title: Offline Reading Shelf Tracker
blocks.purpose: Build a small Node.js application that manages invented reading-shelf records using focused functions, collection transformations, ES modules, automated tests, and an asynchronous JSON-file adapter. This is an educational local exercise, not a production database or multi-user service.
privacy_and_limits: Use invented titles, numeric identifiers, and practice values only; never store real learner names, school records, contact details, or borrowing histories.
Keep files in a temporary or project-local practice directory. Do not connect to Marian, a school system, an account, payment provider, network service, or external API.
A JSON file does not provide transactional concurrent writes, access controls, encryption, backups, or production recovery; document those limitations and do not claim they were solved.
requirements: Represent records with a documented shape including a positive integer id, a trimmed title, and a Boolean availability value.
Write pure functions to normalize a title, validate a record, summarize a collection, and find or update a record without unintended mutation.
Use `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, and a comparator where they improve clarity; demonstrate that source order and data are preserved when the contract requires it.
Put asynchronous JSON file reads and writes behind a small ES module adapter separate from domain rules and command-line output.
Handle a missing optional file as an empty initial collection, but report malformed JSON, invalid record shape, and unexpected filesystem errors distinctly.
Add deterministic Node.js tests for ordinary, boundary, invalid, empty, duplicate-id, and missing-record behavior, including temporary-file adapter checks.
Use `Promise.all` only for independent reads or calculations and document how partial failure and concurrency limits are handled.
Provide a README with Node.js 20+ run/test instructions, data-shape examples, privacy constraints, and explicit non-production storage limitations.
suggested_steps: Write a record contract and draw the flow from file boundary through parsing and validation to normalized domain data.
Implement and test pure transformations before adding any file access.
Separate domain rules, JSON-file adapter, and command-line demonstration into ES modules with one-way dependencies.
Add asynchronous load/save behavior using a temporary practice file; test missing, valid, malformed, and invalid-shape inputs.
Add concurrency and error behavior only where needed; document all-or-nothing versus partial-result decisions.
Review tests, privacy, limitations, instructions, and evidence before presenting the local exercise.
success_checks: Every stored record satisfies the documented shape and invalid records are rejected with a useful non-sensitive error.
Pure transformation functions have deterministic tests and do not unexpectedly mutate source collections.
The file adapter distinguishes missing files from malformed JSON and invalid records; temporary-file tests leave no practice data behind.
The application demonstrates explicit async error handling and does not start unbounded concurrent work.
The README accurately states Node.js requirements, local-only scope, privacy rules, and JSON persistence limitations.

rubric.look_for: Clear pure rules, closures or callbacks where useful, correct transformations, explicit immutability decisions, and edge cases.
Consistent record shape, boundary validation, explicit failure behavior, and normalized internal data.
One-way module responsibilities, deterministic Node.js tests, and observable behavior checks.
Correct promise handling, missing-versus-malformed distinction, safe adapter behavior, and concurrency/failure reasoning.
Reproducible instructions, invented data only, and accurate limits of JSON-file persistence.

revision_notes: Parse JSON, then validate application shape and rules.
Handle missing files separately from malformed data.
Keep storage behind an adapter and do not claim JSON files are a production database.

final_assessment.instructions: Answer twelve multiple-choice questions (4 marks each) and complete both coding tasks (26 marks each). Total: 100 marks. Use invented data and include deterministic tests for normal and invalid cases.

choices.text: The last function that called it
Where code is written and its enclosing scopes

multiple_choice.prompt: What property makes a function pure?

choices.text: Same inputs give the same result without external mutation
A function that cannot be tested
A function that accepts or returns another function
A function with many console messages
A function that only sorts numbers

multiple_choice.prompt: Which collection method selects items matching a predicate?

choices.text: Whether at least one item matches

multiple_choice.prompt: What is important about object spread?

choices.text: It writes the object to disk
It makes a shallow copy, so nested objects may remain shared

multiple_choice.prompt: Why should reusable modules avoid unexpected work at import time?

choices.text: Importers can use and test functions without hidden file or command effects

multiple_choice.prompt: What does a contract-focused test protect?
What must follow JSON parsing for application data?

choices.text: Convert every value to a string
Validate its expected shape and domain rules

multiple_choice.prompt: What does an async function return?

choices.text: A file descriptor in every case

multiple_choice.prompt: When should independent tasks use Promise.all?

choices.text: When their results are all needed together and concurrent execution is appropriate
When each step needs the previous result

multiple_choice.prompt: Why treat malformed JSON differently from a missing optional file?

choices.text: Malformed data may indicate corruption and should not be silently discarded
JSON syntax is the same as authorization
Malformed JSON always means an empty collection
